text: A man drops off a freight car at the edge of a Kansas town on Labor Day morning, and by noon the whole town has an opinion about him. Hal has come to ask a favor of Alan, a college friend whose father owns most of what the train just rolled past, which means the favor is not small and everyone will know it was asked. Almost all of the film stays inside that one holiday: backyards divided by low fences, porches within earshot, a picnic where attendance is close to compulsory. Nothing here is private, which is less a theme than a floor plan. Joshua Logan works by arrangement rather than incident, and the editing prize the film took points to where the effort went, since so much depends on which face is being watched while somebody else is speaking. Heat does the rest.

The money arrives early in the picture, which is what makes the rest of it hard. Five people share a small apartment — Walter Lee Younger, his wife and son, his sister, his mother — and a sum large enough to alter one life is not large enough to alter five. Daniel Petrie keeps the camera close and mostly indoors, so the argument about what the money is for happens where everyone also sleeps, and there is nowhere to go and cool off. Walter Lee has been living like a man serving out a sentence; the windfall lets him speak as though he has plans. So does everybody else. It sits in the National Film Registry, and what holds it there is not the debate but the exactness of the waiting — five people listening to one another finish.

The strike happened in the coal country of West Virginia, and that is where the film was shot, some sixty-odd years later. Joe Kenehan comes in to organize a town whose work, and most of what surrounds the work, belongs to the coal company. The men he needs are divided against each other by design: some were brought in to replace the others, among them a miner called Few Clothes Johnson. Even the mayor and the police chief stand on the wrong side of the local power. John Sayles takes 132 minutes and spends most of them on talk — meetings, arguments about who counts as a brother when any man can be replaced by the next train. Afterwards he published his own account of the shoot, Thinking in Pictures, a director explaining at book length the choices most films leave unexplained.

Daniel Ciello will help the Justice Department clean out the police department on one condition: nobody close to him gets handed over. The condition is the film. Sidney Lumet runs it 167 minutes, and the length is structure rather than indulgence, because a promise like that is not tested in a single scene; it is tested in small rooms, in front of lawyers taking notes, in one more conversation and then one more. Meanwhile the case grows sideways, into narcotics moved through street informants and an arrangement that implicates more of the department than anyone asked to know about. The adapted screenplay was the thing the Academy singled out, which fits a film made almost entirely of testimony, where the decisive act is a sentence somebody agrees to say out loud.

A cashier who has never written a page begins signing his name to other men's scripts. The writers are blacklisted, the work is good, and the arrangement feels at first like a favor done between friends — until it produces a reputation, and the borrowed name acquires a body of work, admirers, and opinions it never had. Martin Ritt keeps the film to 95 minutes and plays much of it for comedy, which is not a softening: the blacklist ran on paperwork, meetings and polite telephone calls, and it is at its worst when everyone involved is being reasonable. Then the pressure shifts from the arrangement to the man inside it. The original screenplay took an Academy Award, and part of what it earns is restraint — the period is never explained, only shown in what people are asked to sign.

A studio producer's day is other people's emergencies, arriving in order. Monroe Stahr handles them, one after another, with the competence of a man who has organized his life so that nothing else can get an appointment. Then a woman he cannot schedule turns up, and the romance that follows is mostly pursuit: messages, near misses, a man accustomed to summoning people discovering that this one keeps being elsewhere. Elia Kazan directs at a temperature well below the material's, which suits a character who conducts his private life as a production. The film won an Academy Award for its design, and that is not incidental — everything Stahr looks at has been arranged, lit and dressed by somebody, including, arguably, the woman. He keeps working at a pace that is visibly costing him.

Seven minutes, one character, and a background that will not stay where it was painted. Daffy Duck goes on performing anyway, which is the joke: he is a professional, and he treats each new indignity — wrong scenery, wrong costume, missing soundtrack, a body redrawn while he is standing in it — as a production problem to be taken up with management. The animator obliges in the worst possible way each time. Chuck Jones made it in 1953, and it now sits in the National Film Registry, which for a cartoon this length is a fair estimate of how much of the medium it dismantles: the brush, the frame edge, the sound, the blank sheet, every part of the apparatus normally kept behind the picture, brought around to the front and used against the duck.

The wedding present arrives in numbered crates: a house in pieces, advertised as a week's work for anyone who follows the instructions. A rejected suitor renumbers the crates. What follows is a comedy of obedience — a man doing exactly as he is told, in the wrong order, at full scale, in real lumber, with a bride watching and a calendar running. Keaton's jokes have to be built before they can be performed, and nothing here can be repaired in the cutting, because the house is genuinely standing there and genuinely wrong. Keaton stays inside the result, which is the whole of the risk. Twenty-five minutes, silent, organized by the days of the week, so the trouble always arrives on schedule. The National Film Registry keeps a copy. The instructions, obeyed to the letter, are the problem.

The hard part is supposed to be the ocean crossing; here it turns out to be the arrival. Chaplin gives the voyage its full measure of misery and then puts his traveler ashore in New York, where the trouble starts at once and takes a different shape: on land, everything has a price, and a man with nothing must still behave as though he belongs. Twenty-four minutes, made in 1917, and the whole thing is conducted in very small sums of money. What keeps it clear of sentiment is timing — the gag lands before the humiliation can settle, which is a mercy and also a refusal to ask for pity. The National Film Registry holds it. It is also, this being Chaplin, a courtship, carried on by a man in no position to pay for one.

The only person in town who understands what is happening is a boy, and the adults he would tell are being changed one at a time. That is a science fiction premise arranged as a domestic one: the invasion is measured not in ruined cities but in the behavior of people at home, still recognizable and no longer reliable. Seventy-eight minutes keeps it at the pitch of a bad dream. The 1953 machinery shows, and was never really the point; what survives is the position the film puts its audience in, which is the boy's position exactly — holding information nobody will accept from a child, watching a familiar street for the small alterations that mean the street is already gone. William Cameron Menzies made horror out of the distance between what children see and what adults will hear.

The Academy still handed out a separate prize for black-and-white photography in 1956, and this film took it. Rocky Graziano's own life supplied the material: trouble with the law long before there was any ring, then the ring as the one line of work that paid for what he already knew how to do. Robert Wise takes his time with the trouble before a bout ever arrives, and the drama that results is less about who wins a fight than about whether a man can walk into a room without his record walking in ahead of him. It is a boxing picture in which the ring is a job rather than a destiny, a place where a man is paid for the thing that used to get him arrested, and the hardest rounds are the ones where nobody is fighting. A hundred and thirteen minutes, and not much ceremony in them.

A safari camp in Kenya, where the party moves on a schedule and nobody can leave early. Victor Marswell hunts for hire. Eloise Kelly turns up as a socialite in transit, and Linda Nordley arrives with her husband, an anthropologist with work to do, which means the triangle assembles itself under canvas with the fourth person present at every meal. John Ford films it as a story about proximity rather than adventure; the animals and the distances are conditions, not events. The two performances the Academy rewarded were the women's, and that seems right, since the hunter is the fixed point and the interest lies in the difference between the two people circling him — one arriving with nothing to protect, the other with a marriage in the next tent.

The man shot during a waterfront robbery did not die of the bullet. A medical examiner finds bubonic plague, which turns a homicide into a public health emergency with a 48-hour clock attached, and the search has to be conducted without telling the city what is being searched for. Elia Kazan works the parts of New Orleans where a stranger passes unremarked: docks, rooming houses, the edges of the shipping trade. The men being hunted do not know what they are carrying. That is the engine of it — a manhunt in which the quarry are also patients, and in which every hour spent explaining is an hour lost. Ninety-six minutes, and the countdown is never staged as a countdown; it is simply the reason nobody in the film is allowed to sleep.

The guest list is settled long before anyone admits how the money is going. A New York socialite plans a dinner of some ambition while her husband, Oliver, works through business trouble he would rather not discuss at the table; across town the Packards, a gruff man and a wife with arrangements of her own, conduct a marriage by negotiation. George Cukor keeps several stories moving through 111 minutes and lets the party work as a deadline: everyone must be dressed and agreeable at the same hour, whatever has happened that afternoon. The year is 1933, and it presses on all of them — these are people whose standing consists of appointments kept and bills not mentioned. The comedy lives in the gap between what has been arranged and what is actually the case.
